Note: the supplied notes array contained five blocks for this paper and five blocks describing a different paper (robust MARL / "curse of multiagency", arXiv:2409.20067); only the Paper A blocks were used, and every answer below was re-verified against the source file. Page numbers are the extraction's page markers (journal pp. 1-15; SI pp. 19-43 = supplementary internal pages 1/24-24/24).
full_citation: Ma, C., Li, A., Du, Y., Dong, H. & Yang, Y. Efficient and scalable reinforcement learning for large-scale network control. Nature Machine Intelligence (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-024-00879-7 (Article; received 18 April 2023, accepted 10 July 2024; code: https://github.com/CDM1619/Networked-MB-MARL).
one_paragraph_summary: The paper develops a model-based decentralized policy-optimization framework ("model-based decentralized policy optimization") for large-scale networked multi-agent systems. Agents live on an undirected graph and use only the states of their κ-hop neighbours (local observation; claimed minimum local message size O(|s_i|), p.3). Each agent keeps a localized dynamics model trained locally by MSE (eq. (6), p.5), performs decentralized PPO with an extended value function V_i(s^{N^κ_i}) (eq. (1), p.3) estimated over κ-hop neighbours (eq. (4), p.3), and runs branched model rollouts to fight compounding model error (p.5). The theory formalizes "ξ-dependent" networked systems with Definitions 1-2 (p.10), proves return bounds for vanilla and T-step branched rollouts and their ξ-dependent generalization (Theorems 1-2, p.10-11; Corollary 1, p.11), and proves that the extended value function and the neighbour-averaged estimate yield value and policy-gradient errors decaying exponentially in κ (Theorems 3-4, eqs. (15)-(17), p.12). Experiments on traffic (New York, up to 436 intersections), power (Real Power-Net up to 421-bus/199 agents) and pandemic networks claim superior sample efficiency, minimal message size, and communication costs about 5-35% of centralized methods (p.5).
problem_setting: Scalable decision-making for large-scale real-world multi-agent network systems (cooperative adaptive cruise control / Flow, adaptive traffic signal control, power grids, pandemic mitigation). Centralized information sharing is infeasible because of communication constraints, cost and privacy (p.1), and independent learning is unstable (p.2); prior model-based MARL relies on a global critic and prior "completely independent system" assumptions are too strong (p.3, SI p.23). The studied setting: n agents on an undirected, stationary graph G=(V,E), each with local state s_i and action a_i; global state/action are concatenations; transitions p(s'|s,a) are Markov; per-agent rewards r_i(s_i,a_i) with global reward the average; objective eq. (7), value eq. (8); each agent may access only its κ-hop neighbours' states, so models, policies and critics are decentralized, with limited communication and limited sampled data (pp.8-10).

answers.q: How does the paper define the scalability problem of centralised learning?
answers.a: The paper gives no formal definition; it frames the scalability problem of centralized learning as three coupled costs. (1) Information/communication: centralized learning requires each agent to have global observations, 'significantly increasing algorithm complexity and communication costs, and reducing scalability' (p.2, Fig. 1a caption), while 'achieving comprehensive information sharing across the entire system becomes unfeasible' owing to communication constraints and high costs, and centralized information collection increases privacy-leakage risk (p.1). (2) Computation/resources: CPPO (a centralized agent with global information) has high theoretical performance but 'due to its dependence on large network size and computing resources, it is difficult to truly achieve theoretical optimal performance'; MAG relies on global modelling information and a global critic, giving 'high computational burden and poor scalability' (p.5; SI p.21: MAG 'is still essentially a centralized training method'). (3) Data: 'the cost of agent–environment interaction rises exponentially with the scale of the system' (p.1), and 'high sample efficiency is also crucial yet unaddressed, rendering current methods effective in only small-scale or simulated environments' (p.3). The paper also notes that prior large-scale MARL handling 500+ agents uses grouping or mean-field approximations, so 'the problem setting remains approximately centralized and cannot address decentralized multi-agent learning in communication-limited scenarios' (p.3).
answers.evidence: p.1: 'achieving comprehensive information sharing across the entire system becomes unfeasible'; 'the cost of agent–environment interaction rises exponentially with the scale of the system'; 'centralized information collection also increases the risk of privacy leakage'. p.2 (Fig. 1a caption): 'centralized learning (left) requires each agent to have global observations, significantly increasing algorithm complexity and communication costs, and reducing scalability'. p.3: 'these approaches often simplify the complexity of large-scale problems through agent grouping or mean-field approximations. The problem setting remains approximately centralized'. p.5: 'due to its dependence on large network size and computing resources, it is difficult to truly achieve theoretical optimal performance'; 'MAG also has high performance ... but leads to high computational burden and poor scalability'. SI p.21: 'This is still essentially a centralized training method, only using local models'.

answers.q: What exactly is wrong with independent learning, in this paper's framing?
answers.a: Independent learning (each agent learning single-agent style from its local observations) reduces system and algorithm complexity but 'the learning process is unstable, leading to poor decision-making performance and mismatch with real-world scenarios' (p.2, Fig. 1a caption). The deeper theoretical complaint is against the prior 'completely independent systems' assumption (INS, Definition 1, p.10: p(s'|s,a) = ∏_i p_i(s'_i | s^{N^κ_i}, a_i)): the authors say this assumption 'is considerably strong and not well-suited for the intricacies of real-world complex systems'; algorithms designed under it 'lack scalability', and 'as the number of agents grows, the approximation errors introduced by this assumption become challenging to control'; additionally, 'due to the absence of model learning, these algorithms exhibit low exploration efficiency and sample efficiency in complex tasks' (SI p.23). The mismatch is quantified as dependency bias D(p||p̄) in the decomposition D(p||p̂) ≤ D(p||p̄) + D(p̄||p̂) (eq. (12), p.10; Definition 2, p.10), and dependency bias 'will increase the generalization error ε_mi of the environment model and policy shift ε_πi between π and π_D, which will further increase the lower bounds C(p,p̂,π,π_D) in Theorems 1 and 2' (p.11); for ξ-dependent systems it adds the additive term 2r_max γ ξ/(1−γ)² to the branched-rollout bound (Corollary 1, p.11). Their corresponding baseline, IMPO, is 'a fully independent model-based MARL method' without neighbour information or the extended value function, and performs worse (p.5; SI p.22).

SI p.23: 'we believe that this assumption is considerably strong and not well-suited for the intricacies of real-world complex systems. Algorithms designed under such an assumption lack scalability ... As the number of agents grows, the approximation errors introduced by this assumption become challenging to control. Furthermore, due to the absence of model learning, these algorithms exhibit low exploration efficiency and sample efficiency'. p.10: Def. 1 (INS) and Def. 2 (ξ-dependent), eq. (12) 'D(p ∥ p̂)≤ D(p ∥ p̄)+D(p̄ ∥ p̂)'. p.11: dependency bias 'will increase the generalization error εmi ... and policy shift επi ... which will further increase the lower bounds C(p, p̂,π,πD) in Theorems 1 and 2'. p.5: 'IMPO is a fully independent model-based MARL method'.

answers.q: What is the networked MDP formulation (state, action, transition, reward, neighbourhood)?
answers.a: pp.8-9 (Methods). A system of n agents is modeled as an undirected, stationary graph G = (V, E); V = {1,...,n} is the set of agents, edges E represent connectivity, and agents 'can communicate along the edges with their adjacent agents'. Neighbourhood sets: N_i = neighbours of i including itself; N^κ_i = the κ-hop neighbour set (graph distance ≤ κ); N^κ_{-i} = N^κ_i excluding the agent (the extraction garbles the set-difference symbol, printing 'N^κ_{-i} = N^κ_i'); adjacency matrix A (n×n) with A_ij = A_ji = 1 iff adjacent, else 0, 'determined by the system structure and κ'. The networked MDP is the tuple (G, {S_i, A_i}_{i∈V}, p, r): each agent has local state s_i ∈ S_i and action a_i ∈ A_i; the global state is the concatenation s = (s_1,...,s_n) ∈ S = S_1×...×S_n and likewise the global action a = (a_1,...,a_n); transition p(s'|s,a) ∈ Δ(S) 'satisfies Markov properties'; each agent maintains a localized policy π_θi(ai|s_Ni) depending only on states of itself and its neighbours, with joint policy π_θ(a|s) = ∏_i π_θi(ai|s_Ni); per-agent reward r_i(s_i,a_i) depends only on local state and action, and the global reward is the average r(s,a) = (1/n) Σ_i r_i(s_i,a_i); objective π_θ* = argmax_πθ E[Σ_{t≥0} γ^t r(s_t,a_t)] (eq. (7), γ ∈ (0,1)) and value function V^{πθ}(s) = (1/n) Σ_i V_i(s) (eq. (8)). This is a formal definition, not a theorem.
answers.evidence: p.9: 'n agents coexist in an undirected and stationary graph G = (V,E)'; 'Let Ni denote the neighbour of the agent i including itself'; 'Aij = Aji = 1' if adjacent, 'determined by the system structure and κ'; 'The global state is the concatenation of all local states: s = (s1,…, sn)'; 'the state transition satisfies Markov properties'; 'Each agent maintains a localized policy πθi i(ai|sNi) ... dependent on only states of its neighbours and itself'; 'ri(si, ai), and the global reward function is defined to be the average reward r(s,a) = (1/n) Σ ri(si,ai)'; eqs. (7)-(8).

answers.a: p.9 (Methods): 'Let N^κ_i denote the κ-hop neighbour of i, that is, the nodes whose graph distance to i is less than or equal to κ.' N_i denotes the neighbours of i including itself, and N^κ_{-i} is defined as N^κ_i minus the agent itself (the set-difference symbol is lost in the extraction, which prints 'N^κ_{-i} = N^κ_i'). κ corresponds to the neighbour 'order' in Fig. 1 (1st/2nd/3rd...), and 'a larger κ implies a broader communication range' (p.2, Fig. 1 caption). The adjacency matrix A is 'determined by the system structure and κ' (p.9). The κ-hop neighbourhood is the conditioning set of the extended value function V_i(s^{N^κ_i}) (eq. (1), p.3), the neighbour set for the localized models p̂_i(s'_i | s^{N^κ_i}, ai) (eq. (11), p.10), and the set defining the local observation s^{N^κ_i} in Algorithm 2 line 5 (p.11). Formal definition, not a theorem.

answers.a: The paper never gives a numbered definition of 'local observation'; it is used operationally and equals the states of the agent and its κ-hop neighbours, s^{N^κ_i}. Algorithm 2, line 5 (p.11): 'Sample action according to decentralized π_θi and local observation s^{N^κ_i} in environment to collect trajectories'. p.9 defines the localized policy as 'dependent on only states of its neighbours and itself'. Fig. 1 (p.2, caption): centralized learning requires global observations, whereas in this method 'each agent receives the state observation from its neighbours and aggregates them with its state and action to obtain the final decision-dependent information'; the abstract (p.1) frames this as 'local observation through the agent-level topological decoupling of global dynamics', claiming accurate estimation of global information. The justification that neighbour states suffice is the locality/exponential-decay property: 'with the increase of the topological distance, the influence between agents will gradually decrease in networked systems' (p.10, citing refs 41, 70; verified empirically in Ring Attenuation, SI Fig. 6, p.33), and in power grids 'the influence diminishes as the distance between nodes increases' (SI p.26).

answers.q: What is the extended value function and how does local information approximate the global value?
answers.a: Definition (eq. (1), p.3): V_i(s^{N^κ_i}) = E_{s^{N^κ_{-i}}}[ Σ_{t≥0} γ^t r_i^t | s_0^{N^κ_i} = s^{N^κ_i} ] — the expected discounted sum of agent i's rewards given only the κ-hop neighbourhood state, with the expectation marginalizing over non-neighbour states. The paper asserts (p.3): 'Vi(s^{N^κ_i}) is a good approximation of Vi(s), with the discrepancy decreasing exponentially with κ (according to Theorem 3).' Theorem 3 (p.12, eq. (15)) formalizes this: with V_i(s^{N^κ_i}) as above and V_i(s) = E[Σ γ^t r_i^t | s_0 = s], |V_i(s) − V_i(s^{N^κ_i})| ≤ r_max/(1−γ) · γ^κ. Remark 1 (eq. (16)) upgrades it to the global value: since V(s) = (1/n) Σ_i V_i(s), |V(s) − (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n V_i(s^{N^κ_i})| ≤ r_max γ^κ/(1−γ), 'which indicates that the global value function V(s) can be approximated by the average of all extended value functions' (p.12). In practice an agent cannot get distant agents' value functions and uses only its κ-hop neighbours: Ṽ_i = (1/n) Σ_{j∈N^κ_i} V_j(s^{N^κ_j}) (eq. (4), p.3; p.12), which is used to build the advantage (p.4). The proof (SI §4.5, p.36) rests on a cited result (ref. 14, Qu/Wierman/Li): fixing the κ-hop states and actions, changes in arbitrarily distant states/actions change the Q-function by at most r_max γ^κ/(1−γ); taking the expectation over actions gives Theorem 3.
answers.evidence: p.3 eq. (1) and: 'Note that Vi(sNκ i) is a good approximation of Vi(s), with the discrepancy decreasing exponentially with κ (according to Theorem 3)'. p.12: Theorem 3, eq. (15) '|Vi(s)−Vi(sNκ i)| ≤ rmax/(1−γ) γκ'; Remark 1, eq. (16) '|V(s)− 1/n Σ Vi(sNκ i)| ≤ rmax/(1−γ) γκ'; 'an agent might not get the value function of distant agents and can access only the value function of its κ-hop neighbours. However, we can prove that Ṽi = 1/n Σj∈Nκ i Vj(sNκ j) is already very accurate for calculating the policy gradient for agent i'. SI p.36 (§4.5): 'if sNκ i and aNκ i are fixed, then no matter how distant states and actions changes, Q-function will not change significantly ... ≤ rmax/(1−γ) γκ'.

answers.q: How does local information approximate the global policy gradient (which theorem, what bound)?
answers.a: Theorem 4 (p.12, eq. (17)). Let Â_t = r^(t) + γV(s^(t+1)) − V(s^(t)) be the TD residual and g_i = E[Â ∇_θi log π_i(a|s)] the (true) policy gradient. When V(s) is replaced by the neighbour-averaged extended value estimate Ṽ_i(s) = (1/n) Σ_{j∈N^κ_i} V_j(s^{N^κ_i}) (as displayed in the theorem; the introducing paragraph on the same page writes V_j(s^{N^κ_j})), with Ã_t and g̃_i the corresponding TD residual and gradient, then |g_i − g̃_i| ≤ γ^{κ−1}/(1−γ) · [1 − (1 − γ²)^{|N^κ_i|/n}] · r_max · g_max, where r_max and g_max bound the absolute reward and gradient (p.12). The error therefore decays exponentially in κ and is further reduced as the κ-hop neighbourhood fraction |N^κ_i|/n grows. Remark 2 (p.12): 'Theorem 4 justifies that the policy gradients computed based on the sum of the neighbouring extended value functions is a close approximation of true policy gradients. The power of this theorem is that the extended value function Vi(sκ Ni) requires only the neighbouring information, thus easier to approximate and scalable.' The paper similarly announces on p.11 that 'the policy gradient induced by equation (5) is an asymptotic approximation of the true policy gradients', and on p.3 that this establishes 'the theoretical bridge between model learning and monotonic policy improvement'. Proof: SI §4.6 (pp.36-37) splits g_i − g̃_i = L1 + L2, bounds L2 ≤ (|N^κ_i|/n)·γ^{κ+1}/(1−γ)·r_max·g_max and L1 ≤ (1 − |N^κ_i|/n)·γ^{κ−1}/(1−γ)·r_max·g_max, and combines them into eq. (17).

If Ãt and g̃i are the TD residual and policy gradient when value function V(s) is replaced by Ṽi(s)=1/n Σj∈Nκ i Vj(...), we have: |gi − g̃i| ≤ γκ−1/(1−γ) [1−(1−γ2)^{Nκ i/n}] rmax gmax, (17) where rmax and gmax denote the upper bound of the absolute value of reward and gradient'. (23)-(24) and final line '= γκ−1/(1−γ) [1−(1−γ2)|Nκ i|/n] rmax gmax'.

answers.q: What is the tradeoff controlled by kappa between performance, communication, computation and approximation error? State the direction of each.
answers.a: As printed in the paper: (1) Policy performance — larger κ gives higher performance on policy training (p.5: 'In general, larger κ leads to higher performance on policy training, but also more communication costs'); the authors read this off Theorems 3 and 4 as 'a larger κ leads to a lower model error, higher sample efficiency and better convergence of episode reward' (p.6). (2) Communication — larger κ increases communication costs (p.5), consistent with 'a larger κ implies a broader communication range' (p.2). (3) Computation — larger κ increases computation overhead (p.10: 'larger κ leads to better approximation of model p, but also heavier computation overhead') because it 'results in more complex models or policy architectures, thereby complicating the training process' (p.5). (4) Approximation/model error — two printed directions must be kept distinct. Formal: the approximation errors in Theorems 3-4 decrease with κ (γ^κ and γ^{κ−1} factors, eqs. (15)-(17), p.12), and 'larger κ leads to better approximation of model p' (p.10). Empirical (κ ablation, p.5): with fixed network structure, sample efficiency increases and measured state-prediction error increases with κ up to a point, after which sample efficiency decreases and prediction error increases 'due to the limited fitting ability of the network'; the observed optimal κ is 4 (Ring Attenuation) and 3 (CACC Catch-up), and in Ring Attenuation 'the information of neighbours under κ = 1 is sufficient for policy learning' (p.6). This empirical statement is in apparent tension with the p.6 theorem-attributed sentence; both are as printed. The paper's own configuration uses κ=1 in seven scenarios and κ=2 in Eight Ring and ATSC (SI Table 3, p.28), with C++PPO treated as the κ = 'arbitrarily huge' limit (SI p.22). Directions, explicitly: performance ↑ with κ (claimed); communication cost ↑ with κ; computation cost ↑ with κ; formal approximation error ↓ with κ; measured prediction error ↑ (initially) and then ↑ with worse sample efficiency (empirical).
answers.evidence: p.5: 'In general, larger κ leads to higher performance on policy training, but also more communication costs. In algorithms, computation cost cannot be overlooked, as larger κ results in more complex models or policy architectures, thereby complicating the training process.' p.10: 'larger κ leads to better approximation of model p, but also heavier computation overhead.' p.6: 'According to Theorems 3 and 4, a larger κ leads to a lower model error, higher sample efficiency and better convergence of episode reward.' p.5 (κ ablation): 'the sampling efficiency will increase and the error of our model in predicting the state will increase with increasing κ. But when κ is greater than a certain value, the sampling efficiency will decrease and the error of our model in predicting the state will increase due to the limited fitting ability of the network. The optimal choice of κ is 4 under our network structure in Ring Attenuation and 3 in CACC Catch-up.' p.2 (Fig. 1 caption): 'a larger κ implies a broader communication range.' SI p.28 (Table 3, row κ): 1 in seven scenarios, 2 in Eight Ring and ATSC.

answers.a: p.5: 'To perform decentralized model-based learning, each agent maintains a localized model. This localized model observes the state of its κ-hop neighbours and its own action, with the goal of predicting the next time step's information, including state and reward.' Formally ŝ_{i,t+1} = p_ψi(s_Ni,t, a_i) with neural-network parameters ψ_i; each agent stores its data locally; models are trained by minimizing the MSE loss L(ψ_i) = (1/|B|) Σ_{τ∈B} ||ŝ_{i,τ+1} − s_{i,τ+1}||² (eq. (6), p.5). The model is itself an INS: p̂(s'|s,a) = ∏_{i=1}^n p̂_i(s'_i | s^{N^κ_i}, a_i) (p.10, used as the 'p̂' in Theorems 1-2 and Corollary 1). Architecture/training (SI §3.1, p.28): separate embedding layers for state and action features aggregated over the graph topology ('this graph network architecture inherently approximates networked Markov Decision Processes'); supervised multi-step extrapolation in batches with real and model-generated data blended at a scheduled ratio (warm start on real data, then a rising share of virtual data) plus a self-supervised correction from real-vs-virtual disparity; 'model fitting and strategy improvement are alternating'. Linear vs nonlinear fitters (SI §3.2, p.29): linear models x_{k+1} = Ax_k + Bu_k + C can suffice for simple tasks but have low fitting efficiency/high variance; nonlinear neural networks are recommended for complex large-scale tasks. Method/definition, not a theorem.

answers.q: How is model-based learning used for sample efficiency?
answers.a: Mechanism: well-learned localized models predict future states and rewards, and predictions are broadcast over local communication, so the agents can generate large amounts of synthetic experience between real interactions (p.3: 'we use well-learned localized models to predict future states and use local communication to broadcast their predictions'; p.10: 'Then our method can use the large amount of data generated by the interaction between the model and the agent to improve the sampling efficiency in the training process'). This matters because 'the cost of agent–environment interaction rises exponentially with the scale of the system' (p.1). Model-based learning is also tied to the monotonic-improvement theory: the return difference between the true environment and the model is bounded as η[π] ≥ η̂[π] − C(p, p̂, π, π_D) (eq. (10), p.10, first given in single-agent MBPO), so 'if every policy update ensures an improvement of η̂[π] by at least C, η[π] will improve monotonically' (p.10). Empirically (pp.5, SI pp.28-30, n=5 statistics): 'the usage of the model will greatly increase the amount of experience to support training and improve the exploration efficiency', and 'our method significantly improves sample efficiency and achieves the highest sample efficiency, converging within 1 × 10−5 training steps, exceedingly outperforms baselines' (as printed on p.5; the exponent is almost certainly an OCR drop for 1 × 10^5 — figure axes read Step (×10^4) up to ~20, i.e. ~2×10^5 steps). The sample-efficiency benefit itself is an empirical claim; only the return-gap condition (eq. (10)) and Theorems 1-2/Corollary 1 are formal.

SI p.30: 'from the training process, we can conclude ... that our method has the highest sample efficiency'.

answers.q: What is branched rollout and why does it help?
answers.a: Definition (p.5): to mitigate the negative effects of model error, the paper adopts a branched rollout scheme (refs 54, 68): 'the model rollout does not start from an initial state, but from a state randomly selected from the most recent environmental trajectory τ. In addition, the model rollout length is fixed to T.' p.10: vanilla rollout assumes models are used in an infinite horizon; 'the branched rollout performs a rollout from a state sampled by a state distribution of previous policy πD, and runs T steps in π̂ according to π'. Why it helps (formal): under vanilla rollout, Theorem 1's model-error coefficient Σ_{k=0}^{∞} γ^{k+1}|N_i^k|/n 'would be in the same magnitude as 1/(1−γ) ... making the bound too loose to be effective' (p.10). Theorem 2 (p.11) for the T-step branched rollout splits the bound so model error ε_mi is weighted only over k = 0..T−1 and policy divergence ε_πi over k = T..∞: 'branched rollout scheme reduced the coefficient before εmi from Σ_{k=0}^{∞} γ^{k+1}|N_i^k|/n ≤ γ/(1−γ) to Σ_{k=0}^{T−1} γ^{k+1}|N_i^k|/n ≤ γ(1−γ^T)/(1−γ). This reduction explains that empirically, branched rollout brings better asymptotic performance. Also, if we set T = 0, this bound turn into a model-free bound. This indicates that when εmi is lower than επi allowed by our algorithm, a model might increase the performance.' (p.11). Empirical support (p.5): rollout lengths 1, 25, 50, 100, 200 tested; the model is accurate enough at short lengths but 'the accuracy of model drops significantly when the rollout length is 200'. The scheme itself is a method (inherited from MBPO-style work); its justification is the formal Theorem 2, corroborated by the ablation.
answers.evidence: p.5: 'the model rollout does not start from an initial state, but from a state randomly selected from the most recent environmental trajectory τ. In addition, the model rollout length is fixed to T.' p.10: 'The branched rollout performs a rollout from a state sampled by a state distribution of previous policy πD, and runs T steps in π̂ according to π'; the vanilla coefficient 'would be in the same magnitude as 1/(1−γ) ... making the bound too loose to be effective'. p.11 (Theorem 2 vs Theorem 1): 'reduced the coefficient before εmi from ... γ/(1−γ) to ... γ(1−γT)/(1−γ)'. p.5 (ablation): 'the accuracy of model drops significantly when the rollout length is 200'.

answers.q: What is compounding model error and how is it controlled?
answers.a: Definition (p.5): 'Scaling model-based methods to real tasks can lead to decreased performance, even if the model itself is relatively accurate. A primary reason for this is the compounding modelling error during long model rollouts, where errors accumulate along the rollout trajectory, ultimately making it inaccurate.' Formal manifestation: in a ξ-dependent system the one-step TV gap between real and model state-action distributions accrues ξ per step, giving DTV(p^t || p̂^t) ≤ DTV(p^0 || p̂^0) + tξ (SI eq. (19), p.35), which in the Corollary 1 proof yields L1 ≤ 2r_max Σ_t γ^t·tξ = 2r_max γ ξ/(1−γ)² (SI eq. (20), p.36); and Lemma 4 (SI p.39) bounds the N-step state-distribution distance by Σ_{t=0}^{N−1} Σ_{j∈N_i^t}(ε_πij + ε_mj) — local model error compounds over the horizon and spreads over the growing neighbourhood. Controls designed by the authors (p.12): (1) 'a stage of warm-up in our algorithm to pre-train the model until an acceptable accuracy'; (2) 'a method to select data from the true MDP or model with a probability'; (3) 'a k-branched rollout method to improve the accuracy of model'; (4) designing 'a distribution of the neighbours for each agent, including the quantity and topology of neighbours, to reduce the model error εmi caused by dependency bias'; (5) PPO trust-region-like policy updates 'to constrain the policy shift επi between π and πD'. The branched rollout bounds model error to T steps (Theorem 2, p.11; SI Lemma 5, p.40: model errors enter only in the k < T sums, pre-branch errors after T), and empirically short rollout lengths (1-100) work while 200 degrades (p.5). These controls are algorithmic designs (plus the formal bounds that quantify the effect); the description itself is the authors' explanation, not a theorem.
answers.evidence: p.5: 'A primary reason for this is the compounding modelling error during long model rollouts, where errors accumulate along the rollout trajectory, ultimately making it inaccurate.' p.12: 'we design a stage of warm-up in our algorithm to pre-train the model ... and a method to select data from the true MDP or model with a probability ... we further adopted a k-branched rollout method to improve the accuracy of model ... we design a distribution of the neighbours for each agent ... Lastly, to constrain the policy shift επi ... we use the method of PPO'. SI p.35, eq. (19): 'DTV (pt(s,a)∥ p̂t(s,a)) ≤ DTV (p0(s,a)∥ p̂0(s,a)) + tξ'. answers.q: Why does this let the method scale to very many agents? Give the concrete largest scale in the experiments.
answers.a: Claimed reasons (all as the paper argues them): (1) Only neighbour information is needed — each agent 'accurately estimates the global value and policy gradient solely through its neighbours' information' (p.2, Fig. 1 caption), justified by Theorems 3-4 whose errors decay exponentially with κ (p.12); (2) the minimum local message size O(|s_i|) (p.3; SI Table 1, p.21, where the method's listed local message size is O(|s_i|), the smallest; caveat: the extracted table lists 6 algorithms with only 5 size expressions, so per-algorithm alignment is partly lost and only the final O(|s_i|) is safely attributable); (3) models, policies and value functions are all decentralized (p.5; SI p.21: unlike MAG, which is 'still essentially a centralized training method'), so no global critic is required; (4) communication cost is about 5-35% of centralized methods (p.5; SI Table 3, p.28, reductions of 65-95% per scenario; only 10% in the large-scale real tasks, SI p.30); (5) model-based learning improves sample efficiency (p.3, p.5), which matters because interaction cost rises exponentially with scale (p.1); (6) the method avoids the approximately-centralized shortcuts (agent grouping / mean-field) used by prior 500+-agent works (p.3). Concrete scales: 'agent counts reaching 199 and 436' (p.3); the New York road network with 436 controllable intersections (p.7; SI Table 2, p.24: '436 different traffic intersections'); Real Power-Net expanded to 322-bus (22 agents) and 421-bus (199 agents) (p.8); Power Grid 20- and 40-agent systems (p.9, Fig. 6 caption); pandemic societies of 500-10,000 people (SI pp.24, 27; 1,000- and 10,000-people societies in Fig. 4c, p.7). The largest concrete agent number in the experiments is therefore 436 (New York traffic intersections); the discussion claims effectiveness 'when the system size scales up to the hundreds of agents' (p.8). Note the source itself prints both 436 (pp.3, 7; SI p.24) and 432 (Fig. 5 caption, p.8) for the New York network. These scale claims are empirical; the enabling approximation guarantees are Theorems 3-4.
answers.evidence: p.3: 'with agent counts reaching 199 and 436'; 'our method significantly surpasses previous decentralized MARL methods in terms of the number of agents it can handle'. p.7: 'the New York City road network with 436 controllable intersections'. p.8: 'When we expand the system scale to 322-bus (22 agents) and 421-bus (199 agents) ... Our method still maintains effective policies, which demonstrate its scalability'; 'remains effective even when the system size scales up to the hundreds of agents'. SI p.24 (Table 2): 'We examined the performance at 436 different traffic intersections'. p.3: 'our method can achieve the minimum local message size O(|si|)'. p.5: 'communication costs ... only about 5-35% of that in centralized methods'. p.8 (Fig. 5 caption): 'New York traffic network with 432 traffic lights'.

answers.q: Which of the above are THEOREMS and which are empirical claims? Be explicit -- do not present an empirical observation as a theorem.
answers.a: FORMAL (theorems/corollaries/remarks with proofs or stated results): Theorem 1 — vanilla-rollout return bound (p.10, eq. (14)); Theorem 2 — T-step branched-rollout return bound and the ε_mi coefficient reduction from γ/(1−γ) to γ(1−γ^T)/(1−γ) (p.11; proof SI §4.3); Corollary 1 — the same bound plus the dependency-bias term 2r_max γ ξ/(1−γ)² for ξ-dependent systems (p.11; proof SI pp.35-36); Theorem 3 — |V_i(s) − V_i(s^{N^κ_i})| ≤ r_max γ^κ/(1−γ) (p.12, eq. (15); proof SI §4.5, p.36); Remark 1 — global-value form, eq. (16) (p.12); Theorem 4 — policy-gradient error bound, eq. (17) (p.12; proof SI §4.6, pp.36-37); Remark 2 — interpretation restating Theorem 4 (p.12). Supporting formal results in the SI: Lemmas 1-6, including Lemma 4 (N-step distribution distance, SI p.39), Lemma 5 (branched-rollout returns bound, SI p.40), Lemma 6 (full-length rollout, SI p.41). Definitions 1-2 (INS and ξ-dependent system, p.10), the networked MDP/kappa-hop/localized-policy definitions (p.9) and the localized-model formulation (eq. (6), p.5) are formal definitions/method specifications, not theorems. EMPIRICAL / INTERPRETIVE (not theorems): the sample-efficiency claim and the 'converging within 1 × 10−5 training steps' figure (p.5; exponent almost certainly OCR-dropped); the communication-cost percentages 5-35% (p.5) and 10% (SI p.30) and Table 3 reductions (SI p.28); the rollout-length ablation (p.5); the κ ablation, the optimal κ = 4/3 values and κ = 1 sufficiency (pp.5-6); the interpretation that 'by using an extended value function, a centralized algorithm can be decomposed into a decentralized algorithm, but the performance would not drop significantly' (p.5); the baseline comparisons (CPPO/DPPO/IMPO/MPOna/MAG, pp.5, SI p.22); all execution results — CACC headway 20 m / velocity 15 m/s (p.7), ATSC queue lengths and delays (p.8), pandemic mortality 0.8-1.5% (p.7), Power-Grid and Real Power-Net results (pp.8-9); the measured ξ ≈ 0.2 (CACC) and ≈ 0.8 (Real Power-Net) (p.4, Fig. 2 caption; SI pp.29-30, eq. (6)); scale numbers 199/436 (p.3, p.8; SI p.24); the six-degrees-of-separation discussion (p.8); and the 'the experimental results are consistent with the theoretical results' sentences on pp.5-6, which are the authors' interpretations of experiments, not theorem statements. Caution on two printed items: the p.5 ablation sentence (measured state-prediction error increases with κ) and the p.6 sentence attributing the opposite direction to Theorems 3-4 are both in the text; the theorem content itself (eqs. (15)-(17)) concerns approximation-error bounds, while the sample-efficiency/reward-convergence claims and the κ optima are empirical.

limitations: Caveats found while re-reading the source (this is not a limitations section of the paper): (i) The theory assumes INS or ξ-dependent structure (Definitions 1-2, p.10); the claim that the evaluated systems 'have the properties of an ξ-dependent system' (p.10) is asserted, and ξ is only empirically estimated for CACC (≈0.2) and Real Power-Net (≈0.8) in SI §3.3 (pp.29-30). (ii) The theorem statements use quantities not defined anywhere in the extraction: |N_i^k| in Theorems 1-2 and the ratio |N^κ_i|/n as an exponent in Theorem 4. (iii) Internal inconsistencies in the printed/extracted math: eq. (4) as extracted divides by n while summing over N^κ_i; Theorem 4's Ṽ_i display on p.12 renders V_j(s_{N_i^κ}) whereas the introducing paragraph on the same page uses V_j(s_{N_j^κ}); the Fig. 2 caption (p.4) and SI eq. (6) print 'ξ ≥ 0.2 / ξ ≥ 0.8' where '≤' is almost certainly intended (both places print ≥); the New York network size is printed as 436 in pp.3, 7 and SI p.24 but 432 in the Fig. 5 caption (p.8); the sample-efficiency figure '1 × 10−5 training steps' (p.5) is inconsistent with the figure axes (Step ×10^4 up to ~20) and is almost certainly OCR-dropped (probably 1 × 10^5). (iv) The 'experimental results are consistent with the theoretical results' sentences (pp.5-6) are the authors' interpretations; the printed text contains a tension between the p.5 empirical κ-ablation (state-prediction error increases with κ until network fitting limits) and the p.6 theorem-attributed direction. (v) Algorithm 3 is referenced on p.5 but no Algorithm 3 box exists in the extraction (possibly in Supplementary Code 1). (vi) Experiment statistics are n = 5 box/bar summaries throughout. (vii) No sample-complexity or communication lower bounds are proved; the scaling benefits are relative to baselines on selected scenarios. (viii) Theorems 1-2/Corollary 1 give lower-bound-style guarantees (η ≥ η̂ − C) whose tightness depends on unquantified constants and on the model and policy errors of the specific run; the paper does not verify the bounds numerically.
